newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs could miss out on aid -- diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs could miss out on aid -- diplomats.

text.p: The United States and European allies have warned Bosnian Serb leaders that they risk missing out on postwar aid if they fail to abide by previous agreements on economic laws, diplomats said on Tuesday.

Envoys from major powers delivered the warning to the Serb member of the country's collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, late on Monday evening after the Serbs withdrew their support for draft economic legislation.
"It was a very tough meeting," said one diplomat, who asked not to be named. "We made clear they would be losing out on an important opportunity. The ball is now in their court."

The Serbs stand to lose hundreds of millions of dollars worth of reconstruction funds if they renege on agreements on a package of laws considered pillars of a reunited peacetime state of Bosnia, diplomats said.

The Serb reversal was the first test of a new initiative by major powers to force Moslem, Croat and Serb nationalists to make good on their commitments under the Dayton peace agreement, which ended their 1992-95 war.
The United States, European powers and Russia declared at a summit last month in Sintra, Portugal, that further financial aid would depend on compliance with the peace treaty.

The international community had required the adoption of laws on a central bank, joint currency, customs and state budget as a condition for holding a conference to raise funds to rebuild Bosnia's shattered infrastructure.
Diplomats said they believed indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic had played a role in the decision to withdraw support for the laws.
Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, told reporters that Krajisnik stuck to his hardline stance in talks with diplomats on Monday.
"President Krajisnik did not move one centimetre. You see the influence of the hidden persuader there," said Murphy, referring to Karadzic.
Murphy said the donors' conference, which has been delayed for months due to disputes over the economic laws, would be held at the end of month as scheduled, with or without the Serb leadership.
"The donors' conference is not the bailiwick of two people, it belongs to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is needed by all of Bosnia-Herzegovina," he said.
Diplomats were concerned that conditionality may not provide much leverage over hardline nationalist Serb leaders, who waged war in order to dismember the Bosnian republic.

Bosnia's postwar Serb entity has received only about two percent of some $2 billion in international aid because the leadership refused to attend a donors' conference last year as part of a joint Bosnian delegation.

Serb ministers last week renounced support for a harmonisation of custom rates between the country's Moslem-Croat Federation and the Serb Republic. They said an agreement on mutual cooperation with neighbouring Serbian-led Yugoslavia took precedence over the customs law.

Western governments say the cooperation pact between Bosnia's Bosnian Serb republic and Yugoslavia carries no legal validity as it was negotiated without approval from Moslem and Croat partners in the Sarajevo government.
Krajisnik reversed his position last week and refused to sign an agreement on a draft central bank law drawn up by U.S. mediators. His Moslem and Croat counterparts have signed the agreement.
